AlgoSB 2026: Learning Protein Dynamics

Dynamic Reweighting for Unbinding Processes

Flavor text for introducing model systems for unbinding processes such as the simple Lennard-Jones cluster in either 2D or 3D. In this exercise, we simulate the unbinding process of a target atom from the model of a Lennard-Jones (LJ) cluster. First, we introduce the this version of setting up a cluster in either 2D or 3d Cartesian coordinate system. Then we define the LJ pair potential parameters and set up the potential instance to compute the potential energy and forces acting on the cluster atom for any given position array. With both, the cluster and potential (force field) instance, we show how to perform a structure optimization and to simulate the unbinding process by classical molecular dynamics using a stochasting integrator with constant temperature. For the start, let us import all the required modules for this exercise. Note the sys.path.insert(0, '../') command which adds the parent directory ( '../' ) to the beginning ( 0 ) of the PYTHONPATH environmental variable, which is a list of directories for Python to search for modules.

Here, 2D clusters does not just mean an initial configuration of atoms within the same plane, but rather that all atom movement only happens on this (x,y)-plane. Even though it is a significant simplificication, the physics stays the same and it increased the visual clarity. In the 2D cluster, a number of atoms cluster_num_atoms are equidistantly distributed on circles with radii cluster_radii . Each atom is assigned a species label which has no relation to the real chemical symbol as all atom and atom pair properties such as atom mass and interaction strength are later individually defined per species (only the colors when displayed are determined by the species).

For a 3D cluster, you also need to define lists for the number of atoms per sphere with certain radii and the atom types. Here the atoms are distributed on the sphere either according to the vertices (corners) of Platonic solids with 4 atoms are distributed like the vertices of a tetrahedron, 6 -> octahedron, 8 -> cube, 12 -> isocahedron or 20 -> dodecahedron. For any other number of atoms, they are distributed with respect to a Fibonacci lattice on a sphere (e.g. https://observablehq.com/@meetamit/fibonacci-lattices)

Now that we have the opportunity to model an initial 2D or 3D LJ-cluster, we assign the respective initial positions, species, number of atoms and coordinates. Note, that marimo does not 'like' variables with the same name but in different cells, so don't hesitate to assign detailed variable names which can be easily understood. The potential model of a LJ cluster is defined by the sum of atom pair potentials with respect to the atom pairs distances. Here, we ask provide the next to the LJ potential D1.LJ1 also a repulsive Weeks-Chandler-Andersen (WCA) potential D1.WCA1 (the 1 indicates the 1-dimensionality, distances, of the potentials). Mathematically they are described by VLJ = 4ε [ ( σ r ) 12 - ( σ r ) 6 ] = ε [ ( rmin r ) 12 - 2 ( rmin r ) 6 ] and VWCA = { VLJ   for   r<rmin 0   for   r≥rmin with r as the atom pair distance and LJ parameters ε and σ with rmin = 2 6 ·σ ≈ 1.12σ . In this implementation, the potential is defined by a dictionary cluster_1d_potentials where the keys are a tuple of two atom species between which a 1D potential acts that is defined in the item. The item is a list where the first element is the 1D potential class ( D1.LJ1 or D1.WCA1 ) and the following elements are the potential parameter. The most significant definition will be the potential between the center atom C and the leaving atom N which is defined here as LJ potential with a potential depth of 10.0 kJ/mol and a σ value of 0.20 nm.

data.text/markdown: Before we start dynamics simulations, we optimize the cluster structure with repsect to its potential energy. Even though the atom masses are not required for the optimization, they can be used to mark atoms to be fixed in space. Physically, an atom can be fixed by increasing its mass to infinity. Technically, it is easier to set the mass of fixed atoms to zero (e.g. as done in openmm). TASK Optimize your cluster and, eventually, adjust your potential parameters or cluster build to achieve a suitable configuration where the center and leaving atom are still bonded and surrounded by 'solvent' atoms.
